rejected.title: The fundamental theorem of calculus
card: Differentiating and integrating undo each other. If F′(x) = f(x), then F is an antiderivative of f.
To find a definite integral, find an antiderivative F, then work out F(b) − F(a). The constant of integration cancels, so leave it out.
Worked example: ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx. An antiderivative of 2x is x². So the integral = 3² − 1² = 9 − 1 = 8.
The same rule works the other way. The derivative of ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt is f(x). Where f is positive, the integral is the area under the curve.
rejected.remember: Integral from a to b of f = F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f.

a.q: What is the value of ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx?
a.why: An antiderivative of 3x² is x³. The integral is 2³ − 0³ = 8. Using the value 3x² = 12 at x = 2 is the tempting mistake, because that is the function's value, not F(2) − F(0).
a.clue: Find F first, then work out F(2) − F(0).

b.q: Mia finds that an antiderivative of 2x + 1 is F(x) = x² + x. What is ∫ from 1 to 4 of (2x + 1) dx?
b.why: F(4) = 16 + 4 = 20 and F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2, so the integral is 20 − 2 = 18. Working out F(1) − F(4) gives −18, but the rule is F(b) − F(a): the value at the lower limit is taken away from the value at the upper limit.
b.clue: Use the upper limit first, then take away the value at the lower limit.
